sentences.text: Sofia was eleven, and she was in the small Galician town of Sarria at eight in the morning on a Tuesday in May, standing at the beginning of a path that ended one hundred kilometers away in the great cathedral of Santiago de Compostela.
She had a small backpack.
She had a wooden walking stick.
She had a scallop shell tied to her backpack strap with a piece of red cord.
The scallop shell was the ancient symbol of a pilgrim on the Camino, and Sofia was, this week, a pilgrim.
Beside her stood her Aunt Marisa.
Marisa was her father's younger sister.
She was forty-three.

She was thin — thinner than she should have been — and she wore a soft cotton headscarf over her head because her hair, which had been dark and long, was now growing back short and gray after eight months of chemotherapy.
Aunt Marisa had breast cancer.
It was, at the moment, in a kind of quiet phase — she had had one round of treatment, and the doctors had said she could do this walk if she wanted to, though they had not exactly recommended it.
She would need another round of treatment when she got back.
And after that — the doctors had said they would see.
Nothing was promised.
Nothing was ruled out.
It had been Aunt Marisa's idea.
Six months ago, when her hair had just started to fall out, she had called Sofia on a Sunday afternoon.
She had said, "Sofia.
I want to walk the Camino de Santiago.
The last hundred kilometers.
From Sarria to Santiago.
I have always wanted to.
And I want you to come with me.
Just you.
Not your parents.
Not your uncle.
Just us." Sofia had been surprised.
She had said, "I am eleven, Aunt Marisa." Aunt Marisa had said, "Yes.
That is why I want you.
I want to walk it with someone who has not seen most of what I have seen.
I want to walk it with someone who is looking at the world for the first time.
Also — I love you.
I want to spend a week with you before the next round of treatment."
Sofia's parents had had a long conversation about it.
Her mother had been worried.
Her father had said, "Marisa is right.
Sofia should go.
It will be good for both of them." The doctors had agreed.
And so, six months later, on a warm May morning, Sofia stood in Sarria with her aunt, ready to begin.
Aunt Marisa turned to her.
She said, "Ready?" Sofia said, "Yes." Aunt Marisa said, "Buen Camino." And they started walking.
The Camino was a path — it had been a path for over a thousand years.
Pilgrims from all over Europe had walked to Santiago since the ninth century, when the bones of the apostle James were said to have been found there.
Sofia had known this from school.
She had thought of it as an ancient religious thing.
But when they walked out of Sarria that first morning, she saw that it was still a very living thing.
There were other pilgrims on the path — not many at this hour, but a steady trickle.
Some old, some young.
Some in groups.
Some alone.
Some with heavy packs, some with light packs.
All of them wearing scallop shells.
All of them going the same direction, west.
The path went out into the Galician countryside.
It was very green.
There were low stone walls on both sides of the path.
There were fields with cows.
There were small oak woods.
Every so often the path went through a small village of stone houses with slate roofs — three or four houses, a cow in a yard, a small chapel, a fountain.
Then out again into the fields.
Sofia had never seen anywhere like this.
She had lived her whole life in Madrid, in a city.
This — a whole country of small quiet green places — was new to her.
"How are you feeling," Aunt Marisa asked, after about an hour.
"Good," said Sofia.
"How are you feeling." Marisa smiled.
She said, "I am tired.
But I am the good kind of tired.
I have not walked much in eight months.
My legs have forgotten.
But my heart is happy.
Both are true." They walked in silence for a while.
Then Marisa said, "I want to tell you something, Sofia.
I do not want you to worry, on this walk, about my — my health.
I know you know I am sick.
That is a fact.
But this week is not about my sickness.
This week is about — walking.
About us being together.
About the small things we see.
If I need to rest, I will rest.
If I need to say something, I will say it.
But I do not want you to be careful with me.
I want you to be an eleven-year-old on a long walk.
Can you do that."
Sofia thought.
She said, "Yes.
I can try." Marisa said, "Good.
If I am too much aunt today, tell me.
And if you are too much eleven-year-old, I will tell you.
We will just — walk."
They walked twenty kilometers that first day.
They stopped in a small village called Portomarín.
There was a pilgrim's albergue — a hostel — where any pilgrim with a shell could stay for a few euros a night.
It was a plain place.
There were bunk beds in a big room.
There was one shared bathroom.
There was a small kitchen.
Marisa and Sofia found their bunks.
They set down their packs.
Marisa lay down for a while — she was tired, but not in a bad way — and Sofia went for a small walk around the village.
In the evening they ate supper together at a small pilgrim's restaurant that had a set menu for six euros — soup, chicken and rice, an apple, a small glass of wine for Marisa and water for Sofia.
They ate at a long table shared with four other pilgrims — an older German couple, a young French woman walking alone, and a middle-aged man from Ireland who did not talk much.
Everyone was tired.
Nobody talked a great deal.
But there was a small warm feeling around the table.
Everyone was walking to the same place.
Everyone had walked the same twenty kilometers today.
Everyone would walk more tomorrow.
There was a solidarity in it that did not need to be spoken.
